notaTipos: Not a slip: they take different types. [iconDef] takes the icon's whole definition — its geometry plus its animation variants. [icon] takes the shape to morph INTO.
verEnApi: See both in the API reference →
notaSpring: spring takes a preset name. The full list, with the damping value behind each one, is in the API reference — it isn't copied here so the two can't drift apart.
intro: The icon grid shows what's there. This shows what it's for: controls that actually do what they say — the copy one copies, the theme one changes colors, the send one has its three states. Each one's code sits right next to it.

copiar.descripcion: The case where morph clearly wins: copy → check confirms without shifting the layout or bolting on a toast. The button above actually copies — try it and paste.
copiar.detalle: If writeText fails (no permission, no focus, site on http) the state doesn't change: the icon stays on copy instead of lying with a checkmark.

tema.descripcion: moon ↔ sun. The icon inherits the text color (stroke="currentColor"), so the theme never has to touch it directly: change the container's color and the icon follows.
tema.detalle: Here the theme only applies to this panel, so the pattern reads in isolation. The real one lives in the header, with the same morph: it writes data-theme on <html>, remembers your choice, and reveals the new theme with a circle that grows out of the button itself.

enviar.descripcion: Idle → sending → sent, and back again. send → circle-check via morph; the spinner is a curated <gf-icon> on loop.
enviar.detalle: The spinner is a curated <gf-icon> on loop; the check is a morph. Two engines, one button.

reaccion.descripcion: There's no morph here: the shape doesn't change, only the gesture. trigger="tap" replays the heart's curated choreography on every click, and the button supplies the color.
reaccion.detalle: The heart keeps its shape — only the gesture changes, so the choreography engine is the whole job.

menu.descripcion: Two different shapes for one control. The icon says what the button does now, not what it is.
menu.detalle: The trigger owns aria-expanded, and Esc closes returning focus to it. Without that, Escape leaves focus on the <body> and the next Tab restarts from the top of the page.

play.descripcion: The same control, two shapes. aria-pressed carries the state; the morph only carries the change.
play.detalle: Not a spinner and not a swap: the triangle becomes the two bars. If it just swapped, the eye would read it as two buttons instead of one that changed.

acordeon.descripcion: This one is not morph, and that is the point: the shape does not change, it rotates.
acordeon.detalle: A shape-interpolation engine to turn 180° is paying for a problem you do not have. A CSS transform does it, honours prefers-reduced-motion with three lines, and ships zero bytes of runtime.

campana.descripcion: Nothing to transition to: the shape stays the same and the movement carries the meaning.
campana.detalle: That is what separates the two engines. Morph needs a destination shape; choreography needs a reason to move. Here there is no second shape — a bell that rang is still a bell.

buscar.descripcion: The field expands and the icon announces what the button will do next.
buscar.detalle: While collapsed the input is out of the tab order (tabindex="-1"): a field nobody can see should not be a stop for someone navigating by keyboard.

decision.mezcla: Mixing them isn't sloppiness. The three-state send button uses both: a looping choreography while it does not know when it will finish, and a morph the moment it does.

forma.ejemplos: menu → X · play → pause · search → close
forma.porque: Two shapes, one control. The morph carries the change so the eye reads one button, not two.

reacciona.porque: Nothing to transition to. The shape stays and the movement carries the meaning.

duracion.porque: A morph has a start and an end. "Loading" has neither, so it needs an animation that cycles.
